analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and social service employers to write and carry out plans to protect workers from violence.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 37 senators, never got a vote; it was referred to a Senate committee on April 18, 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Health care and social service workers face some of the highest rates of workplace violence of any occupation — from patients, clients, and visitors. This bill would have ordered the Labor Department to write a federal safety standard requiring hospitals, nursing homes, emergency responders, home health agencies, and similar employers to assess risks, set up prevention plans with employee input, investigate incidents, keep records, train staff, and protect workers who report violence. It also would have tied Medicare participation for some hospitals and nursing homes to following the standard. The bill was introduced with 37 Senate sponsors but never received a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses, aides, emergency responders, home health aides, social workers, and other staff in hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, and community care settings, who would gain enforceable protections against violence at work — including staffed teams, alarms, barriers, training, and anti-retaliation rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care and social service workers

how_it_helps.text: Each covered employer would have to develop a written workplace violence prevention plan, built with the participation of direct-care employees, tailored to the specific hazards of each facility and work unit.

Plans must include engineering and work-practice controls — alarm systems, secure access, staffing levels, security personnel, de-escalation training — plus procedures to report, investigate, and correct violent incidents.

Employers would have to keep a violent incident log for at least five years, train employees annually, submit annual reports to the Labor Department, and could not retaliate against workers who report threats or incidents.
Hospitals and skilled nursing facilities not otherwise covered by federal workplace safety law would have to comply with the standard as a condition of participating in Medicare.
The Labor Department would have to issue an interim standard within one year and a final standard within 42 months, prioritizing technical assistance to employers during an initial compliance period.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, psychiatric and substance-use treatment centers, and other covered employers, which would bear the cost of risk assessments, security controls, staffing changes, training, and recordkeeping. Indirectly, some costs could pass through to patients and payers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and care providers

drawbacks.text: The bill fast-tracks the rule: the interim standard would skip the usual detailed rulemaking requirements of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and executive-order regulatory review, allowing only a 30-day comment period before it takes effect — a real good-faith objection that such a sweeping standard would get less scrutiny than normal.

Covered employers would carry substantial compliance costs — engineering controls like metal detectors and access systems, added security staffing, and heavy recordkeeping and annual reporting duties — for facilities already operating on thin margins, especially nursing homes and rural hospitals.

The definition of workplace violence is broad, covering threats and incidents regardless of whether an employee is injured, which could generate significant documentation burdens and liability exposure for providers of care to confused or combative patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Health care workers face violence rates far above other workers, and the bill's core mechanism — employer prevention plans built on OSHA's own 2015 guidelines, with employee participation and enforceable reporting — is a well-established approach already used in some states. The honest costs are the compliance burden on care providers and the unusually fast rulemaking track, which trades procedural scrutiny for speed. On balance, the protections are concrete and the costs fall mainly on employers in a sector with documented violence problems, but the rushed timeline is a legitimate design criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on April 18, 2023, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill in the Senate on April 18, 2023, joined by 37 cosponsors, all Democrats or the independent Senator Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other health care employers avoided a federal workplace violence standard and its compliance costs; health care workers got no new federal protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care employers; workers gained nothing

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the Labor Department to issue a workplace violence prevention standard for health care and social service employers.

for.name: 37 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 36 Democrats and 1 Independent, including Sen. Sanders and Sen. Casey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it committee-ready support, though no Republican cosponsor signed on.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 118th Congress by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no floor vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 supporters were Democrats or one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and with the Senate evenly divided the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and long-term care facilities
industries.note: They would bear the cost of prevention plans, security controls, training, and recordkeeping, and some would have had to comply as a condition of Medicare participation. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the safety protections workers sought.
Field work like home health care is explicitly covered, requiring risk assessments and prevention plans for workers in private homes — settings that are hard to control with engineering measures.
Emergency services and transport, including firefighters and emergency responders, fall within covered services and would need to meet the standard.

industries.industry: Psychiatric, substance-use treatment, and community care providers
industries.note: Psychiatric facilities, drug treatment centers, group homes, and mental health clinics are covered facilities and would carry the same plan, training, and logging requirements.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing and employee leasing firms
industries.note: Contractors, subcontractors, and temp firms employing workers in covered settings count as covered employers and would share compliance duties, though the bill requires coordination among employers sharing a worksite.
